claim: Importin-9 is made up of twenty tandem HEAT repeats.
source: Imp9 is made up of twenty tandem HEAT repeats, each containing two antiparallel helices A and B that line the convex and concave surfaces of superhelical-shaped protein, respectively (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural organization of Imp9 based on the crystal structure, with reference to figures showing the structure.

claim: Each HEAT repeat of Importin-9 contains two antiparallel helices A and B that line the convex and concave surfaces of the superhelical-shaped protein.
source: Imp9 is made up of twenty tandem HEAT repeats, each containing two antiparallel helices A and B that line the convex and concave surfaces of superhelical-shaped protein, respectively (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural organization of HEAT repeats based on the crystal structure.

claim: The concave surface of Importin-9 is mostly acidic, with a few small basic patches.
source: The concave surface of Imp9 is mostly acidic, with a few small basic patches (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the electrostatic properties of Imp9's surface based on structural analysis.

claim: The charged concave surface of Importin-9 wraps around H2A-H2B.
source: This charged concave surface of Imp9 wraps around H2A-H2B, burying 1352 Å2 (26% of the H2A-H2B surface) at three distinct interfaces 1–3 (Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the interaction between Imp9 and H2A-H2B based on the crystal structure.

claim: Importin-9 buries 1352 Å2 of H2A-H2B surface area, which represents 26% of the H2A-H2B surface.
source: This charged concave surface of Imp9 wraps around H2A-H2B, burying 1352 Å2 (26% of the H2A-H2B surface) at three distinct interfaces 1–3 (Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements of the buried surface area from structural analysis.

claim: Importin-9 and H2A-H2B interact at three distinct interfaces.
source: This charged concave surface of Imp9 wraps around H2A-H2B, burying 1352 Å2 (26% of the H2A-H2B surface) at three distinct interfaces 1–3 (Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural organization of the Imp9-H2A-H2B interface based on the crystal structure.

claim: The Importin-9-bound H2A-H2B has a canonical histone-fold as in nucleosomes.
source: The Imp9-bound H2A-H2B has a canonical histone-fold as in nucleosomes (151 Cα atoms aligned, r.m.s.d. 0.505 Å; PDB ID 1AOI) (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript compares the structure of H2A-H2B in the Imp9 complex to the nucleosome structure, providing alignment statistics.

claim: 151 Cα atoms of Imp9-bound H2A-H2B align with nucleosomal H2A-H2B with an r.m.s.d. of 0.505 Å.
source: The Imp9-bound H2A-H2B has a canonical histone-fold as in nucleosomes (151 Cα atoms aligned, r.m.s.d. 0.505 Å; PDB ID 1AOI) (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative structural alignment data comparing Imp9-bound H2A-H2B to nucleosomal H2A-H2B.

source: In our structure, the N-terminal and C-terminal tails of H2A (residues 1–16, 101–130) and H2B (1-27, 125-126), the first 14 residues of Imp9 and its H19loop (residues 936–996) were not modeled due to missing electron density.
evidence: The manuscript describes which regions of the structure could not be modeled based on crystallographic data.

claim: The N-terminal tail of H2B (residues 1-27) and C-terminal residues (125-126) were not modeled due to missing electron density.
source: In our structure, the N-terminal and C-terminal tails of H2A (residues 1–16, 101–130) and H2B (1-27, 125-126), the first 14 residues of Imp9 and its H19loop (residues 936–996) were not modeled due to missing electron density.
evidence: The manuscript describes which regions of the structure could not be modeled based on crystallographic data.

claim: The first 14 residues of Importin-9 were not modeled due to missing electron density.
source: In our structure, the N-terminal and C-terminal tails of H2A (residues 1–16, 101–130) and H2B (1-27, 125-126), the first 14 residues of Imp9 and its H19loop (residues 936–996) were not modeled due to missing electron density.
evidence: The manuscript describes which regions of the structure could not be modeled based on crystallographic data.

claim: The H19loop of Importin-9 (residues 936–996) was not modeled due to missing electron density.
source: In our structure, the N-terminal and C-terminal tails of H2A (residues 1–16, 101–130) and H2B (1-27, 125-126), the first 14 residues of Imp9 and its H19loop (residues 936–996) were not modeled due to missing electron density.
evidence: The manuscript describes which regions of the structure could not be modeled based on crystallographic data.

claim: Interface 1 on Importin-9 comprises the loop that follows helix 2B and the last turns of helices 3B, 4B and 5B.
source: Interface 1 on Imp9 comprises the loop that follows helix 2B and the last turns of helices 3B, 4B and 5B (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1A, 2A and 3A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural composition of Interface 1 based on the crystal structure.

claim: Hydrogen-bonding with H2A-H2B residues caps the C-terminal ends of Importin-9 B helices at Interface 1.
source: Hydrogen-bonding with H2A-H2B residues caps the C-terminal ends of these Imp9 B helices (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript describes specific structural interactions observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The last turn of Importin-9 helix 4B is capped end-to-end by the first turn of histone H2B helix α2.
source: Of note is the end-to-end capping of the last turn of Imp9 helix 4B by the first turn of histone H2B helix α2.
evidence: The manuscript describes a specific structural feature observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Interface 1 on the histones involves α2-L2-α3 of H2A and α1-L1-α2 of H2B.
source: Interface 1 on the histones involves α2-L2-α3 of H2A and α1-L1-α2 of H2B, which constitute a significant portion of the basic DNA-binding surface found in nucleosomes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the histone regions involved in Interface 1 based on the crystal structure.

claim: The histone regions in Interface 1 constitute a significant portion of the basic DNA-binding surface found in nucleosomes.
source: Interface 1 on the histones involves α2-L2-α3 of H2A and α1-L1-α2 of H2B, which constitute a significant portion of the basic DNA-binding surface found in nucleosomes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the functional significance of the histone regions in Interface 1 by comparing to nucleosome structure.

claim: Although histones and Importin-9 surfaces at Interface 1 are electrostatically complementary, interactions also involve many hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions and main chain interactions.
source: Although histones and Imp9 surfaces at this interface are electrostatically complementary (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), interactions also involve many hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions and main chain interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the nature of interactions at Interface 1 based on structural analysis.

claim: Interface 2 involves Importin-9 helices 7B, 8B and the H8loop binding to the short 28KKRRK32 segment of the H2B N-terminal tail.
source: Interface 2 involves Imp9 helices 7B, 8B and the H8loop (connects helices 8A to 8B) binding to the short 28KKRRK32 segment of the H2B N-terminal tail (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplements 1B, 2B–C and and 3B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural composition of Interface 2 based on the crystal structure.

claim: Electron densities for H2B residues 28KKRRK32 are weak.
source: Electron densities for H2B 28KKRRK32 are weak (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C) and atomic displacement parameters ('B-factors') for H2B residues 28–32 are also high (>100 Å2), suggesting dynamic interactions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the quality of electron density for specific residues in the crystal structure.

claim: Atomic displacement parameters ('B-factors') for H2B residues 28–32 are high (>100 Å2), suggesting dynamic interactions.
source: Electron densities for H2B 28KKRRK32 are weak (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C) and atomic displacement parameters ('B-factors') for H2B residues 28–32 are also high (>100 Å2), suggesting dynamic interactions.
evidence: The manuscript interprets high B-factors as evidence for dynamic interactions based on crystallographic data.

claim: Charged H2B side chains at Interface 2 make electrostatic interactions with several acidic Importin-9 residues.
source: Charged H2B side chains make electrostatic interactions with several acidic Imp9 residues, while the aliphatic part of these basic side chains and their backbone participate in hydrophobic interactions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the nature of interactions at Interface 2 based on structural analysis.

claim: The aliphatic part of H2B basic side chains and their backbone at Interface 2 participate in hydrophobic interactions with Importin-9.
source: Charged H2B side chains make electrostatic interactions with several acidic Imp9 residues, while the aliphatic part of these basic side chains and their backbone participate in hydrophobic interactions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the nature of interactions at Interface 2 based on structural analysis.

claim: Interface 3 involves the last three HEAT repeats of Importin-9.
source: Interface 3 involves the last three HEAT repeats of Imp9, specifically the last turn of helix 18A and the short loop that follows, the H18-19loop, the C-terminal half of helix 19A and the first turn of helix 20B (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplements 1C, 2D and 3C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural composition of Interface 3 based on the crystal structure.

claim: At Interface 3, charges are reversed compared to typical importin-cargo interactions, with a basic patch on Importin-9 complementing an acidic surface on the histones.
source: Instead of the typical basic H2A-H2B residues interacting with the acidic Imp9 residues, charges at Interface 3 are reversed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B). A basic patch formed by the Imp9 H18-19loop and nearby helices complement an acidic surface on the histones formed by residues from H2A helices α2 and αC, and the C-terminal half of H2B that comprises α2-α3-αC.
evidence: The manuscript describes the electrostatic properties of Interface 3 based on structural analysis.

claim: Importin-9 residue Arg898 forms salt bridges with several acidic residues of H2A at Interface 3.
source: Of note here are salt bridges between Imp9 residue Arg898 and several acidic residues of H2A (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript describes specific interactions observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Many hydrophobic contacts are found at Interface 3.
source: Many hydrophobic contacts are also found at this interface, and several helices (Imp9 H18A, H19A and histone H2B α2) are capped through hydrogen-bonding with partner proteins (Figure 2—figure supplements 1C and 3C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the nature of interactions at Interface 3 based on structural analysis.

claim: Several helices (Importin-9 H18A, H19A and histone H2B α2) are capped through hydrogen-bonding with partner proteins at Interface 3.
source: Many hydrophobic contacts are also found at this interface, and several helices (Imp9 H18A, H19A and histone H2B α2) are capped through hydrogen-bonding with partner proteins (Figure 2—figure supplements 1C and 3C).
evidence: The manuscript describes specific structural features observed at Interface 3.

claim: Importin-9 binds full-length H2A-H2B with a KD of 30 nM.
source: Imp9 binds full-length H2A-H2B with high affinity (KD = 30 nM).
evidence: The manuscript reports binding affinity measured by ITC experiments.

claim: H2AΔTail-H2B (H2A residues 14–119 with full-length H2B) has similar binding affinity to Importin-9 (KD = 40 nM) as full-length H2A-H2B.
source: H2A-H2B mutant assembled with the core of H2A (residues 14–119) and full-length H2B, hence named H2AΔTail-H2B, has similar binding affinity (KD = 40 nM) as full-length H2A-H2B.
evidence: The manuscript reports binding affinity measured by ITC experiments for a deletion mutant.

claim: The result that H2AΔTail-H2B binds Importin-9 with similar affinity as full-length H2A-H2B is consistent with structural observations that H2A residues in its N- and C-terminal tails are disordered and likely do not contact Importin-9.
source: This result is consistent with structural observations that H2A residues in its N- and C-terminal tails are disordered and likely do not contact Imp9.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the binding data in the context of structural observations.

claim: Removal of the H2B tail (deleting residues 1–35), generating mutant H2A-H2BΔ(1-35), did not affect binding affinity to Importin-9 (KD = 40 nM).
source: Removal of the H2B tail (deleting residues 1–35), generating mutant H2A-H2BΔ(1-35), also did not affect binding affinity (KD = 40 nM).
evidence: The manuscript reports binding affinity measured by ITC experiments for a deletion mutant.

claim: The lack of effect on binding affinity when removing the H2B tail is not surprising given the weak electron density and high B-factors of H2B 28KKRRK32 bound to Importin-9 in Interface 2.
source: This is not surprising given the weak electron density and high B-factors of H2B 28KKRRK32 bound to Imp9 in Interface 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the binding data in the context of structural observations.

claim: H2AΔTail-H2BΔTail (H2A residues 14–119 complexed with H2B residues 25–123) binds as tightly to Importin-9 as the full-length histones (KD = 40 nM).
source: A H2A-H2B mutant dimer with only the core domain (H2A residues 14–119 complexed with H2B residues 25–123; named H2AΔTail-H2BΔTail) also bind as tightly to Imp9 as the full-length histones (KD = 40 nM).
evidence: The manuscript reports binding affinity measured by ITC experiments for a deletion mutant.

claim: Removal of the Importin-9 H8loop (Imp9ΔH8loop) did not decrease binding to H2A-H2B (KD = 10 nM).
source: Removal of the Imp9 H8loop (Imp9ΔH8loop), which forms part of the binding site for H2B 28KKRRK32, also did not decrease binding (KD,Imp9ΔH8loop = 10 nM; Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports binding affinity measured by ITC experiments for a deletion mutant.

claim: The histone tails do not contribute much binding energy for interactions with Importin-9.
source: The histone tails thus do not contribute much binding energy for interactions with Imp9.
evidence: The manuscript concludes based on the binding data from multiple deletion mutants.

claim: Removal of the H18-19loop of Importin-9 reduced the affinity for H2A-H2B 15-fold (KD = 450 nM).
source: Removal of the H18-19loop reduced the affinity 15-fold (KD = 450 nM; Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports binding affinity measured by ITC experiments for a deletion mutant.

claim: An endothermic binding reaction occurred upon truncation of the H18-19loop of Importin-9.
source: We note the endothermic binding reaction that occurred upon truncation of this 40-residue loop.
evidence: The manuscript reports thermodynamic observations from ITC experiments.

claim: The reduction in affinity upon removal of the H18-19loop suggests substantial contribution of Interface 3 to the total binding energy.
source: This result suggests substantial contribution of Interface three to the total binding energy.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the binding data to infer the contribution of Interface 3.

claim: Removal of the H19loop of Importin-9 did not affect affinity for H2A-H2B (KD = 40 nM).
source: Removal of the H19loop did not affect affinity (KD = 40 nM; Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that this disordered loop does not participate in H2A-H2B binding.
evidence: The manuscript reports binding affinity measured by ITC experiments for a deletion mutant.

claim: The disordered H19loop of Importin-9 does not participate in H2A-H2B binding.
source: Removal of the H19loop did not affect affinity (KD = 40 nM; Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that this disordered loop does not participate in H2A-H2B binding.
evidence: The manuscript infers the lack of participation based on the binding data.

claim: A large portion of the Importin-9 interface on H2A-H2B overlaps with the DNA-binding and H3-H4-binding interfaces used in nucleosomes.
source: A large portion of the Imp9 interface on H2A-H2B overlaps with the DNA-binding and H3-H4-binding interfaces used in nucleosomes (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The manuscript compares the Imp9-H2A-H2B interface to the nucleosome structure.

claim: The feature of Importin-9 occluding interfaces used in the nucleosome is common to many H2A-H2B histone chaperones.
source: This feature of Imp9 occluding interfaces used in the nucleosome is common to many H2A-H2B histone chaperones of H2A-H2B (Hammond et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript compares Imp9 to known histone chaperones and cites literature.

claim: Importin-9 buries more surface area on H2A-H2B (1352 Å2) than well-characterized H2A-H2B chaperones such as Nap1 (387 Å2), Swr1 (488 Å2), Anp32e (533 Å2), Chz1 (906 Å2), Spt16 of FACT (185 Å2) and YL1 (883 Å2).
source: Imp9 in fact buries more surface area on H2A-H2B (1352 Å2) than well-characterized H2A-H2B chaperones such as Nap1 (387 Å2), Swr1 (488 Å2), Anp32e (533 Å2), Chz1 (906 Å2), Spt16 of FACT (185 Å2) and YL1 (883 Å2) (Hondele et al., 2013; Hong et al., 2014; Kemble et al., 2015; Luger et al., 1997; Mosammaparast et al., 2002a; Obri et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript compares quantitative measurements from the Imp9 structure to published structures of histone chaperones.

claim: Titration of Nap1 against DNA•H2A-H2B complexes leads to the release of free DNA as Nap1 binds H2A-H2B.
source: Titration of Nap1 or Imp9 against DNA•H2A-H2B complexes leads to the release of free DNA as Nap1 or Imp9 binds H2A-H2B (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from gel-shift assays.

claim: Titration of Importin-9 against DNA•H2A-H2B complexes leads to the release of free DNA as Importin-9 binds H2A-H2B.
source: Titration of Nap1 or Imp9 against DNA•H2A-H2B complexes leads to the release of free DNA as Nap1 or Imp9 binds H2A-H2B (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from gel-shift assays.

claim: The results from gel-shift assays suggest that Importin-9 can act as a histone chaperone by shielding H2A-H2B from promiscuous interactions while it accompanies the histones from the cytoplasm to the nucleus.
source: These results suggest that Imp9 can act as a histone chaperone by shielding H2A-H2B from promiscuous interactions while it accompanies the histones from the cytoplasm to the nucleus.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the gel-shift assay results to infer chaperone activity.

claim: When increasing concentrations of RanGTP are added to an immobilized MBP-Imp9•H2A-H2B complex, the histones are not released.
source: When increasing concentrations of RanGTP (5–30 molar equivalents S. cerevisiae Ran(1–177/Q71L)) are added to an immobilized MBP-Imp9•H2A-H2B complex, the histones are not released (Figure 4A; controls shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from pull-down binding assays.

claim: The RanGTP protein used in the experiments is fully active as it easily dissociates a cargo/NLS from Kapβ2.
source: The RanGTP protein used in these experiments is fully active as it easily dissociates a cargo/NLS from Kapβ2 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from control experiments to validate RanGTP activity.

claim: The Importin-9•H2A-H2B complex remains intact when added to immobilized MBP-RanGTP.
source: In a separate experiment, the Imp9•H2A-H2B complex also remains intact when added to immobilized MBP-RanGTP (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from pull-down binding assays.

claim: MBP-RanGTP binds to H2A-H2B-bound Importin-9 to form a heterotetrameric MBP-RanGTP•Imp9•H2A-H2B complex.
source: MBP-RanGTP binds to H2A-H2B-bound Imp9 to form what seems to be a heterotetrameric MBP-RanGTP•Imp9•H2A-H2B complex (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from pull-down binding assays and interprets the complex stoichiometry.

claim: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays show the formation of a 1:1 complex between Importin-9 and H2A-H2B.
source: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA) show the formation of a 1:1 complex between Imp9 and H2A-H2B (Figure 4D) as well as between Imp9 and RanGTP (Figure 4E, lanes 3–6).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from EMSA experiments.

claim: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays show the formation of a complex between Importin-9 and RanGTP.
source: Electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA) show the formation of a 1:1 complex between Imp9 and H2A-H2B (Figure 4D) as well as between Imp9 and RanGTP (Figure 4E, lanes 3–6).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from EMSA experiments.

claim: A complex containing equimolar amounts of Importin-9, H2A-H2B and RanGTP can form.
source: A complex containing equimolar amounts of Imp9, H2A-H2B and RanGTP can also form (Figure 4E, lanes 7–10).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from EMSA experiments.

claim: Size exclusion chromatography of Importin-9•H2A-H2B in the presence of excess RanGTP shows a large complex that contains Importin-9, H2A-H2B and Ran.
source: Size exclusion chromatography of Imp9•H2A-H2B in the presence of excess RanGTP also shows a large complex that contains Imp9, H2A-H2B and Ran (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from size exclusion chromatography experiments.

claim: Sedimentation coefficient values of individual proteins estimated from sedimentation velocity experiments are consistent with their molecular weights: Importin-9 (3.7S), H2A-H2B (1.3S) and RanGTP (1.4S).
source: Sedimentation coefficient values of the individual proteins estimated from the sedimentation velocity experiments are consistent with their molecular weights: Imp9 (3.7S), H2A-H2B (1.3S) and RanGTP (1.4S).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from analytical ultracentrifugation experiments.

claim: The binary complexes of Importin-9•H2A-H2B and Importin-9•RanGTP have sedimentation coefficients of 4.3S and 4.2S, respectively.
source: The binary complexes of Imp9•H2A-H2B and Imp9•RanGTP are both larger, at 4.3S and 4.2S, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from analytical ultracentrifugation experiments.

claim: The mixture of Importin-9, H2A-H2B and RanGTP gave peaks at 1.4S (excess RanGTP) and 4.6S.
source: The mixture of Imp9, H2A-H2B and RanGTP gave peaks at 1.4S (excess RanGTP) and 4.6S.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from analytical ultracentrifugation experiments.

claim: The 4.6S assembly from the mixture of Importin-9, H2A-H2B and RanGTP is larger than either Importin-9•H2A-H2B or Importin-9•RanGTP and is likely the quaternary RanGTP•Importin-9•H2A-H2B complex.
source: The 4.6S assembly is larger than either Imp9•H2A-H2B or Imp9•RanGTP and is likely the quaternary RanGTP•Imp9•H2A-H2B complex.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the analytical ultracentrifugation results to infer the complex stoichiometry.

claim: Molecular weight of the RanGTP•Importin-9•H2A-H2B complex was estimated to be 161.1 kDa by SAXS MOW.
source: Molecular weight of the RanGTP•Imp9•H2A-H2B complex was estimated to be 161.1 KDa by using SAXS MOW (Fischer et al., 2010) a value nearly identical to the expected molecular weight of 163.2 kDa from the sequence thus confirming stability of the 4-polypeptide chain RanGTP•Imp9•H2A-H2B complex in solution (Figure 4G).
evidence: The manuscript reports molecular weight estimation from SAXS data.

claim: The estimated molecular weight of 161.1 kDa for the RanGTP•Importin-9•H2A-H2B complex is nearly identical to the expected molecular weight of 163.2 kDa from the sequence, confirming stability of the 4-polypeptide chain complex in solution.
source: Molecular weight of the RanGTP•Imp9•H2A-H2B complex was estimated to be 161.1 KDa by using SAXS MOW (Fischer et al., 2010) a value nearly identical to the expected molecular weight of 163.2 kDa from the sequence thus confirming stability of the 4-polypeptide chain RanGTP•Imp9•H2A-H2B complex in solution (Figure 4G).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the SAXS data to confirm the complex stoichiometry and stability.

claim: In structures of different importins bound to RanGTP, RanGTP is always sandwiched between N-terminal and either central or C-terminal HEAT repeats of the importins.
source: In these structures, RanGTP is always sandwiched between N-terminal and either central or C-terminal HEAT repeats of the importins (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript compares multiple importin-RanGTP structures from the literature.

claim: Importin-RanGTP interactions at the first four HEAT repeats of importins appear to be structurally conserved even though the interface on the opposite side of RanGTP involves different central or C-terminal HEAT repeats in different importins.
source: Importin-RanGTP interactions at the first four HEAT repeats of importins (binding Switch 1, Switch two and α3 of RanGTP) appear to be structurally conserved even though the interface on the opposite side of RanGTP involves different central or C-terminal HEAT repeats in different importins (Chook and Blobel, 1999; Kobayashi and Matsuura, 2013; Lee et al., 2005; Tsirkone et al., 2014; Vetter et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript compares multiple importin-RanGTP structures from the literature.

claim: Structural alignment of HEAT repeats 1–4 of Importin-9 with HEAT repeats 1–4 of Importin-β(1-462)•RanGTP shows an r.m.s.d. of 3.27 Å for 152 Cα atoms.
source: Structural alignment of HEAT repeats 1–4 of Imp9 with HEAT repeats 1–4 of Importin-β(1-462)•RanGTP (PDB ID 1IBR (Vetter et al., 1999); r.m.s.d. of 152 Cαs in the alignment is 3.27 Å), Kap95•RanGTP (2BKU (Lee et al., 2005) r.m.s.d. of 152 Cαs in the alignment is 3.20 Å), Kapβ2•RanGTP (1QBK (Chook and Blobel, 1999) r.m.s.d. of 152 Cαs in the alignment is 4.02 Å), Kap121•RanGTP (3W3Z (Kobayashi and Matsuura, 2013); r.m.s.d. of 144 Cαs in the alignment is 2.51 Å), Transportin-SR2•RanGTP (4C0Q; (Maertens et al., 2014) r.m.s.d. of 144 Cαs in the alignment is 5.02 Å) and Importin-13•RanGTP (2 × 19 (Bono et al., 2010); r.m.s.d. of 144 Cαs in the alignment is 3.29 Å), and examination of the six structures at a single orientation of Imp9, show that RanGTP binds in very similar orientations to very similar locations at the N-terminus of these importins (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–F).
evidence: The manuscript reports structural alignment results comparing Imp9 to other importins.

claim: Structural alignment of HEAT repeats 1–4 of Importin-9 with HEAT repeats 1–4 of Kap95•RanGTP shows an r.m.s.d. of 3.20 Å for 152 Cα atoms.
source: Structural alignment of HEAT repeats 1–4 of Imp9 with HEAT repeats 1–4 of Importin-β(1-462)•RanGTP (PDB ID 1IBR (Vetter et al., 1999); r.m.s.d. of 152 Cαs in the alignment is 3.27 Å), Kap95•RanGTP (2BKU (Lee et al., 2005) r.m.s.d. of 152 Cαs in the alignment is 3.20 Å), Kapβ2•RanGTP (1QBK (Chook and Blobel, 1999) r.m.s.d. of 152 Cαs in the alignment is 4.02 Å), Kap121•RanGTP (3W3Z (Kobayashi and Matsuura, 2013); r.m.s.d. of 144 Cαs in the alignment is 2.51 Å), Transportin-SR2•RanGTP (4C0Q; (Maertens et al., 2014) r.m.s.d. of 144 Cαs in the alignment is 5.02 Å) and Importin-13•RanGTP (2 × 19 (Bono et al., 2010); r.m.s.d. of 144 Cαs in the alignment is 3.29 Å), and examination of the six structures at a single orientation of Imp9, show that RanGTP binds in very similar orientations to very similar locations at the N-terminus of these importins (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–F).

evidence: The manuscript reports observations from fluorescence microscopy and cites supporting data from the Human Protein Atlas.

claim: Similar cytoplasmic localization of Importin-9 was reported in the Human Protein Atlas.
source: We also show by fluorescence microscopy that Imp9 in these cells localizes mostly to the cytoplasm (Figure 1B). Similar cytoplasmic localization of Imp9 was reported in the Human Protein Atlas (Thul et al., 2017; Uhlen et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites data from the Human Protein Atlas.

claim: The crystal structure of human Importin-9 bound to full-length X. laevis H2A-H2B was solved by single wavelength anomalous dispersion to 2.7 Å resolution.
source: To understand how Imp9 recognizes histones for nuclear import, we solved the crystal structure of human Imp9 bound to full-length X. laevis H2A-H2B (dissociation constant, KD = 30 nM; Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) by single wavelength anomalous dispersion to 2.7 Å resolution (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the method and resolution of structure determination.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) of human Importin-9 binding to full-length X. laevis H2A-H2B is 30 nM.
source: To understand how Imp9 recognizes histones for nuclear import, we solved the crystal structure of human Imp9 bound to full-length X. laevis H2A-H2B (dissociation constant, KD = 30 nM; Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) by single wavelength anomalous dispersion to 2.7 Å resolution (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the binding affinity measured by ITC.

claim: Importin-9 shows Importin-9-histone interactions in immunoprecipitation from the cytoplasmic fraction of a stable HeLa cell line expressing mCherry-H2B.
source: We show Imp9-histone interactions in immunoprecipitation from the cytoplasmic fraction of a stable HeLa cell line expressing mCherry-H2B (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Nucleosomes are structural and functional units composed of 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped around two H3-H4 dimers and two H2A-H2B dimers.
source: Eukaryotic chromatin is organized into nucleosomes, which are structural and functional units that are composed of 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped around two H3-H4 dimers and two H2A-H2B dimers (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about nucleosome structure from the literature.

claim: Nucleosomes are assembled in the nucleus during S-phase as new H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 proteins are synthesized in the cytoplasm.
source: Nucleosomes are assembled in the nucleus during S-phase as new H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 proteins are synthesized in the cytoplasm (Adams and Kamakaka, 1999; Annunziato, 2012; Verreault, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about nucleosome assembly from the literature.

claim: Newly translated histones are folded and assembled into H2A-H2B and H3-H4 dimers, which are then imported into the nucleus for deposition onto replicating chromatin.
source: Newly translated histones are folded and assembled into H2A-H2B and H3-H4 dimers, which are then imported into the nucleus for deposition onto replicating chromatin.
evidence: The manuscript describes the process of histone trafficking based on established knowledge.

claim: Despite their small sizes, histones do not diffuse into the nucleus but are transported by nuclear import receptors of the Karyopherin-β family termed importins.
source: Despite their small sizes, histones do not diffuse into the nucleus but are transported by nuclear import receptors of the Karyopherin-β family termed importins (Baake et al., 2001; Jäkel et al., 1999; Johnson-Saliba et al., 2000; Mosammaparast et al., 2002b; Mosammaparast et al., 2001; Mühlhäusser et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on histone nuclear import.

claim: Importins usually recognize their protein cargos by binding nuclear localization signals (NLSs) in their polypeptide chains.
source: Importins usually recognize their protein cargos by binding nuclear localization signals (NLSs) in their polypeptide chains.
evidence: The manuscript describes the typical mechanism of importin-cargo recognition based on established knowledge.

claim: Importins bind nucleoporins to traverse the permeability barrier of the nuclear pore complex (NPC).
source: Importins bind nucleoporins to traverse the permeability barrier of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) (reviewed in Chook and Süel, 2011; Cook et al., 2007; Görlich and Kutay, 1999; Izaurralde et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2018; Kosinski et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2016; Soniat and Chook, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites reviews on nuclear transport mechanisms.

claim: The small GTPase Ran controls direction of transport.
source: The small GTPase Ran controls direction of transport.
evidence: The manuscript describes the role of Ran based on established knowledge.

claim: Binding of cargos and RanGTP to importins is mutually exclusive.
source: Binding of cargos and RanGTP to importins is mutually exclusive.
evidence: The manuscript describes the typical behavior of importin-cargo-RanGTP interactions based on established knowledge.

claim: In the nucleus, where Ran is kept in the GTP state by guanine nucleotide exchange factor RCC1, importins bind RanGTP with high affinity, resulting in cargo release.
source: In the nucleus, where Ran is kept in the GTP state by guanine nucleotide exchange factor RCC1, importins bind RanGTP with high affinity, resulting in cargo release (Chook and Süel, 2011; Izaurralde et al., 1997; Soniat and Chook, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the mechanism of cargo release in the nucleus.

claim: Studies in importin-deletion yeast strains identified Kap114 as the primary H2A-H2B importer, and Kap121 and Kap123 as secondary importers.
source: Studies in importin-deletion yeast strains identified Kap114 (S. cerevisiae homolog of Importin-9 or Imp9) as the primary H2A-H2B importer, and Kap121 (homolog of Importin-5) and Kap123 (homolog, Importin-4) as secondary importers (Mosammaparast et al., 2002b; Mosammaparast et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on histone importers in yeast.

claim: Pull-down binding from cytosolic HeLa extract and proteomics tracking nuclear-cytoplasmic localization in human cells identified core histones as Importin-9 cargos.
source: Pull-down binding from cytosolic HeLa extract and proteomics tracking nuclear-cytoplasmic localization in human cells also identified core histones as Imp9 cargos (Jäkel et al., 2002a; Kimura et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on Imp9 cargos in human cells.

claim: Many previous studies have shown that H2A and H2B can bind and be imported into nuclei of digitonin-permeabilized cells by several human importins in addition to Importin-9.
source: The use of multiple backup importin systems is also seen in human cells, as many previous studies have shown that H2A and H2B can bind and be imported into nuclei of digitonin-permeabilized cells by several human importins (such as Importin-β, Karyopherin-β2, Importin-4, Importin-5, Importin-7) in addition to Importin-9 (Baake et al., 2001; Johnson-Saliba et al., 2000; Mosammaparast et al., 2002b; Mosammaparast et al., 2001; Mühlhäusser et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on multiple importins that can import H2A-H2B.

claim: Core histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 all contain disordered N-terminal tails followed by small histone-fold domains.
source: Core histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 all contain disordered N-terminal tails followed by small histone-fold domains; H2A also has a disordered C-terminal tail (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on histone structure.

claim: H2A also has a disordered C-terminal tail.
source: Core histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 all contain disordered N-terminal tails followed by small histone-fold domains; H2A also has a disordered C-terminal tail (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on histone structure.

claim: The N-terminal tails of histones contain many basic residues, somewhat resembling classical NLS motifs.
source: The N-terminal tails of histones contain many basic residues, somewhat resembling classical NLS motifs (Blackwell et al., 2007; Ejlassi-Lassallette et al., 2011; Johnson-Saliba et al., 2000; Marchetti et al., 2000; Greiner et al., 2004; Mosammaparast et al., 2001; Moreland et al., 1987).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the properties of histone tails.

claim: H2A and H2B tails are able to target heterologous proteins into the nucleus.
source: H2A and H2B tails are able to target heterologous proteins into the nucleus (Mosammaparast et al., 2001), but removal of the tails does not abolish localization of H2A-H2B in the nucleus (Thiriet and Hayes, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the function of histone tails in nuclear localization.

claim: Removal of the H2A and H2B tails does not abolish localization of H2A-H2B in the nucleus.
source: H2A and H2B tails are able to target heterologous proteins into the nucleus (Mosammaparast et al., 2001), but removal of the tails does not abolish localization of H2A-H2B in the nucleus (Thiriet and Hayes, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the function of histone tails in nuclear localization.

claim: Analysis of seven different importins binding to H3 and H4 tails vs. full-length H3-H4 vs. H3-H4•Asf1 chaperone complex suggested that specificities for importin-binding reside not only in the tail 'NLSs' but also in the histone folds and the bound chaperone.
source: Furthermore, analysis of seven different importins binding to H3 and H4 tails vs. full-length H3-H4 vs. H3-H4•Asf1 chaperone complex suggested that specificities for importin-binding reside not only in the tail 'NLSs' but also in the histone folds and the bound chaperone (Soniat et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on importin-histone binding specificity.
